items.prompt: Likes on a celebrity's post arrive at 80 000/s, and the single Redis key holding its like count sits on a shard that is now at 100% CPU while the other shards idle.
items.why: One key, one shard, and a commutative counter → split it into sub-counters (likes:post#0..#N) and sum on read. More shards or a new ring would still put that one key on one node.

items.prompt: A user database of 4 TB and 200 000 writes/s, spread evenly across users, no longer fits on one primary.
items.why: The load is even and the problem is total size and write rate → partition users across nodes. No single key is hot, so splitting individual keys would add nothing.

items.prompt: A buggy partner integration sends 5 000 requests/s with the same API key, crowding out everyone else.
items.why: One client is misbehaving and its traffic should be refused → cap it per API key. A hot key is legitimate demand from many clients for the same item, which you must serve.

items.prompt: During a world-cup final, 3 million viewers poll the same match-score key every 2 s; the score changes a few times per match and a 1 s delay is fine.
items.why: One read-hot key with tolerated staleness → a 1 s in-process cache per app server, plus coalescing on miss. The shared shard then sees one read per server per second, not 1.5 M/s.

items.prompt: One breaking-news article is requested 400 000 times a second; the cache node that owns its key handles about 100 000 ops/s, and the team proposes adding virtual nodes to the hash ring.
items.why: A single key needs 4× one node's capacity → replicate it under key#0..#N or cache it in-process on the app servers. Virtual nodes even out many keys but still place this one key on one node.

items.prompt: Each view of a video runs UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1; viral videos cause lock timeouts on their rows.
items.why: One row takes every increment → shard the counter (or count in memory and flush aggregates). A read cache doesn't help a write-hot row, and a queue alone just moves the same contended update later.

items.prompt: A post by an account with 40 M followers has to appear in all their home timelines within a minute.
items.why: The challenge is one write that must reach 40 M feeds (write amplification) → choose push vs pull per author. That's fan-out, not one overloaded key.

items.prompt: Product pages are read 100× more than they're edited, and every product is about equally popular; the database p99 is too slow.
items.why: Read-heavy with no skew → a shared cache in front of the database. With an even spread, no single key overloads a shard, so the hot-key fixes aren't needed.
